project_name: Pinecrest Mill kraft lignin cake (fictional): dashboard assessment
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: The lignin leaves the mill as wet cake and no lignin dryer is available, so buyers needing dry powder would require drying before use or shipment.
The stream is currently fired in the mill's boilers as internal fuel, so diversion to external sales would affect the existing fuel route.
Solvent or membrane fractionation and chemical modification are not available at the mill, limiting pathways that require those processing steps.
Moisture is uncertain and directly affects dry tonnage and shipping mass, so handling and commercial commitments require moisture verification.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing, limiting qualification against pathways that depend on these properties.
Covered cake storage is limited, so wet-cake dispatch must be coordinated with production and transport.
data_quality_notes: The record is explicitly fictional demo data; every figure is an illustrative assumption rather than a measurement from a real mill.
The reported moisture and composition values are assumptions with stated ranges, and moisture should be measured over time before relying on the dry-mass profile.
The lignin-content analytical method is stated for illustration and should be confirmed before comparison with buyer specifications.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing and require laboratory analysis.
The validation checks passed for dry-matter balance, composition total, and coverage of missing figures; no inconsistencies were reported.
agent.summary: Validated fictional profile: the record describes a wet kraft lignin cake stream with a converted annual wet mass, moisture fraction, and calculated dry mass, but commercial qualification remains limited by the fictional status, unavailable drying and downstream processing, current internal-fuel use, moisture uncertainty, and missing chemical properties.

sulfur_pct.method: Total sulfur by elemental analysis (stated for illustration)

carbohydrates_pct.method: Total sugars after acid hydrolysis (stated for illustration)

data_gaps.impact: Every figure in this profile is invented for demonstration. Results based on it say nothing about a real mill.
data_gaps.next_step: Replace the profile with the mill's own lab data and production records.

data_gaps.impact: Molecular weight can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of molecular weight distribution, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: Phenolic hydroxyl content can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of hydroxyl group content, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: The make-up of the ash is unknown, so ash-related requirements can only be checked against total ash.
data_gaps.next_step: Request an inorganic element analysis of the ash.

data_gaps.impact: Reported lignin content depends on what the analysis counts. The method here is stated for illustration only.
data_gaps.next_step: Confirm the analytical method with the lab and use the same one when comparing with buyers' specifications.

data_gaps.impact: Moisture sets the dry tonnage (dry matter = wet quantity x (1 - moisture)) and the mass that has to be shipped.
data_gaps.next_step: Log cake moisture for each shift over at least one month.

checks.disclaimer: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.

current_use.description: Fictional: the precipitated lignin is fired in the mill's own boilers in place of purchased fuel. The unit was built to relieve the recovery boiler, not to sell lignin.

geographic_market.logistics: Fictional: rail siding at the mill; the nearest deep-water port is assumed to be about 150 km away.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#1: UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins, with typical replacement up to 50% when a two-step depolymerization process is used.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin is supported for veneer plywood and other wood-based-panel adhesives; one producer reports industrially proven resin meeting EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3.
Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before use in the documented PF-resin route.

target_customers.statement: Potential customer types are plywood producers and manufacturers of other wood-based panels using phenol-formaldehyde adhesives.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is phenol used in phenol-formaldehyde resins.

qualification_requirements.statement: The documented plywood application uses EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 as a performance qualification.
Formaldehyde emissions can be assessed using EN 717-2, which is reported for LPF-bonded panels.
The laboratory study assessed viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde against a Chinese wood-adhesive standard, although the source names that standard inconsistently.
The PF route requires activation or depolymerization of kraft lignin before use.

limitations: The replacement levels are summarized from published studies rather than demonstrated in one commercial plant.
The industrially proven and performance claims for LPF resin are vendor claims without a cited test report.
The evidence does not establish that Pinecrest's untreated wet cake meets the documented process or quality conditions.
The documented depolymerized-lignin molecular-weight range is not a stated requirement for mill-delivered lignin.
missing_information: No current lignin price, delivered resin economics, market volume, named buyers, purchase contracts, or regional demand is provided.
No evidence specifies whether a buyer would accept wet cake or would require dried, milled, or otherwise processed lignin.
No evidence confirms Pinecrest lignin's molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, ash, or sodium content for PF qualification.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents an industrially proven plywood resin and established wood-panel adhesive use, but it does not document a commercial sale by a lignin producer or identify buyers. This is stronger than research-only evidence but below the rubric's commercial-sales level.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#2: Replacing 25% of the polyol with lignin cut compressive strength by 40% compared with lignin-free foam; raising lignin from 25% to 60% caused no further drop.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#2: In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Unmodified lignin has been demonstrated as a partial replacement for petroleum-based polyol in rigid PUR/PIR foam; at 30 wt% replacement, 16 of 19 tested lignins passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Rigid foam containing 19-23% hardwood kraft lignin retained comparable structure and strength in a laboratory study, although replacing 25% of polyol reduced compressive strength by 40%.
Kraft lignin has also been tested at 20 wt% replacement in flexible polyurethane foam, but the resulting kraft-lignin foams were denser and stiffer than the organosolv alternatives.

The broader lignin-polyurethane pathway is assessed at TRL 6, and kraft lignin replacement levels in cited studies reached up to about 20% after oxypropylation, up to 50% after depolymerization and oxypropylation, and up to 100% after liquefaction in a bio-based polyol.

target_customers.statement: Potential customer types include rigid insulation-foam producers and other polyurethane foam manufacturers.
Automotive flexible-foam producers are a potential customer type, while the evidence suggests kraft-lignin formulations may be better suited to heavy-duty foams than automotive flexible foam.

competing_materials.statement: The incumbent material is petroleum-based polyol used in polyurethane formulations.

qualification_requirements.statement: For rigid polyurethane foam, total lignin hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g, equivalent to 3.56 mmol/g total hydroxyl groups, is cited as the acceptable range; this is total hydroxyl content rather than phenolic hydroxyl content.
Rigid PUR/PIR foam performance can be qualified against ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Kraft lignin needs significant treatment such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction to reach target polyurethane properties in the documented review.

limitations: Most evidence is from laboratory foam studies rather than commercial production.
The 30 wt% rigid-foam result covers 19 lignins and does not provide a kraft-only pass rate in the cited claim.
The evidence reports poor product consistency, technical performance, and high production costs as commercialization barriers.
The feedstock profile states that chemical modification is unavailable at the mill, which conflicts with the documented treatments for the higher replacement levels.
Pinecrest's total hydroxyl value, moisture, molecular-weight distribution, and formulation behavior are not established.
missing_information: No current lignin price, polyurethane-grade volume demand, named buyers, contracts, or regional demand is provided.
No evidence establishes acceptance of wet lignin cake; drying or other preparation requirements for a buyer are not specified.
No commercial qualification pathway, customer trial, or full-scale production result is documented for Pinecrest lignin.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence shows substantial research interest and a broader TRL 6 assessment, but the pathway evidence is dominated by laboratory studies and reviews; it does not document a commercial lignin-polyurethane sale, buyer, or development partnership.

supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#3: Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#4: Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#3: Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#1: DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).

applications.statement: Lignin is documented as a precursor for carbon fiber, but the cited ORNL precursor specifications require greater than 99% lignin, ash below 0.1%, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and removal of particles larger than 1 µm.

Softwood lignin can provide carbon yields of 55% or more, but it is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; the cited lignin-based carbon fibers reached about 50% of the mechanical-property target in that work.

Lignin-derived hard carbon is documented for sodium-ion battery anodes; kraft-lignin hard carbon carbonized at 1,200 °C had higher initial coulombic efficiency than hard carbon from sulfonated lignin in the reviewed comparison.
Lignin-derived hard carbon is also documented for lithium-ion battery anode material, with a reported pilot line and planned standardized 20 kton manufacturing units in company material.

Activated carbon is the least restrictive documented carbon application because the evidence states that precursor quality has no strict limitations, although higher ash lowers yield and carbon conversion.

target_customers.statement: Potential carbon-fiber customer types include carbon-fiber plants and manufacturers serving automotive applications.
Potential hard-carbon customer types include battery manufacturers and carmakers that qualify anode materials.
The evidence supports activated-carbon producers or users as a potential customer type, but it does not identify a specific end-market buyer.

competing_materials.statement: PAN-based fiber is the named incumbent comparator for carbon fiber.
Anthracite is a named fossil feedstock comparator for sodium-ion battery hard carbon.
Conventional activated carbon is the incumbent material for the activated-carbon application.

qualification_requirements.statement: Carbon-fiber precursor qualification requires greater than 99% lignin content, ash below 0.1% by weight, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and complete removal of particles larger than 1 µm.
The cited kraft lignin for carbon fiber required purification before use, and softwood lignin required a plasticizing or alloying agent for melt spinning.
Battery-material qualification can take 3 years with battery manufacturers and carmakers, according to the cited company material.
Activated-carbon precursor quality has no strict limitations, but lower ash improves yield and carbon conversion.

limitations: The carbon-fiber specifications are cited secondhand and come from a non-kraft lignin study; none of that study's lignins met the volatiles specification.
Carbon-fiber development evidence includes a 2009 progress report and modelled rather than measured costs.
The GreenLight evidence concerns precursor-fiber production at TRL 5, not the complete lignin-to-carbon-fiber chain.
The battery pilot and scale-up information is company investor material from 2021, and later status was not verified.
The activated-carbon evidence is a laboratory study using zinc chloride activation.
The hard-carbon evidence is a review and the stated costs have no specified currency and basis beyond $/t.
missing_information: No current Pinecrest feedstock assay is provided for ash, volatiles, carbohydrates, metals, particle content, or carbon yield.
No current market volumes, purchase prices, named carbon-fiber buyers, activated-carbon buyers, battery-material contracts, or regional demand estimates are provided.
No evidence establishes whether wet cake can be accepted by carbon-material processors or what drying, purification, activation, or carbonization preparation they would require.
No evidence provides a complete commercial qualification result for Pinecrest lignin in any of the three carbon-material subapplications.

market_evidence.rationale: The pathway has documented industrially relevant development: GreenLight reached TRL 5 for precursor-fiber production, and company material reports a battery-material pilot and qualification activity. However, the evidence does not document several producers selling to established buyers, so it does not support scores 4 or 5.

processing_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin must undergo activation or depolymerization before use in the documented phenolic-resin route.
The route would need resin formulation and qualification for wood-panel customers, including EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 and formaldehyde assessment using EN 717-2.
Pinecrest would also need to resolve wet-cake handling because no mill dryer is available and buyer acceptance of wet cake is unconfirmed.
Feedstock compatibility was not scored because the evidence library supplied no numeric requirements for this pathway.

technical_maturity.statement: Biobased phenolic-resin production is assessed at TRL 8, mapping to a high technical-readiness score.

adoption_barriers.statement: The mill lacks the solvent or membrane fractionation and chemical-modification capability that could be needed to prepare lignin for the route, so a processing partner or new equipment would be required.

Customers would need confidence that Pinecrest material can meet panel-adhesive performance and emissions requirements, while Pinecrest molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl, ash, and sodium data are not available.
Potential customers are plywood and other wood-based-panel producers, but no named buyers, contracts, regional demand, current lignin price, or delivered-resin economics are provided.
External sales would compete with the mill's existing boiler-fuel route and require coordinated dispatch because covered cake storage is limited.

assumptions: The economics tool used fictional wet-feedstock assumptions of 36000.0 / 40000.0 / 43000.0 t/yr and moisture assumptions of 40.0 / 35.0 / 30.0% of wet mass across its scenarios.
The economics tool treated dry mass as 26000.0 t/yr dry in the base case, with conservative and optimistic dry-mass values of 21600.0 and 30100.0 t/yr.
No availability fraction, product yield, product price, or variable cost was assumed by the economics tool.
Assessment assumes Pinecrest would need an external activation or depolymerization capability because the mill does not have chemical-modification capability.
Assessment treats diversion from boiler fuel as a commercial tradeoff rather than assuming all dry mass is saleable.
uncertainties: The indicative economics could not calculate usable feedstock, product output, revenue, variable cost, gross contribution, or contribution per tonne because required inputs were missing.
The compatibility result does not test Pinecrest against numeric PF specifications; missing composition data may materially affect qualification.
The TRL evidence describes the technology broadly and does not establish commercial qualification of Pinecrest lignin.
Moisture uncertainty may change dry tonnage, shipping mass, and whether wet-cake dispatch is practical.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: This route has high reported technology readiness, but Pinecrest would need activation or depolymerization, qualification testing, drying or a wet-cake-accepting buyer, and a route that replaces existing boiler-fuel use. It therefore needs major new processing capability and an external partner rather than only modest additions to existing assets.

processing_requirements.statement: For carbon-fiber precursor use, lignin content must exceed 99%, ash must be below 0.1% by weight, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and particles larger than 1 µm must be removed.
The documented kraft lignin carbon-fiber route requires purification, and softwood lignin requires a plasticizing or alloying agent for melt spinning.

Activated carbon is less restrictive on precursor quality, although lower ash improves yield and carbon conversion; hard-carbon and carbon-fiber routes still require application-specific carbonization and qualification.

The deterministic feedstock check scored compatibility at 1 for the checked carbon-fiber requirements: the profile shows lignin content of 94 versus a minimum above 99 and ash of 1 versus a maximum of 0.1.

Pinecrest would need a drying and preparation route because it produces wet cake, while processor acceptance of wet cake and required purification, activation, or carbonization preparation are not established.

technical_maturity.statement: Lignin precursor fiber production is reported at TRL 5, mapping to an intermediate technical-readiness score.

adoption_barriers.statement: Carbon-fiber use faces strict precursor specifications and a measured feedstock gap in lignin purity and ash, while volatiles, carbohydrates, particle content, metals, and carbon yield are not provided for Pinecrest.

The mill lacks fractionation and chemical-modification capability, and carbon-material processors may also require purification, activation, high-temperature carbonization, or specialized spinning equipment.
Battery-material qualification can take 3 years with battery manufacturers and carmakers, creating a substantial adoption cycle for hard-carbon products.
Potential customers span carbon-fiber plants, battery manufacturers, carmakers, and activated-carbon users, but no named buyers, contracts, market volumes, or purchase prices are provided.
External diversion would affect the mill's boiler-fuel route, and limited covered storage makes wet-cake dispatch dependent on coordinated production and transport.

buyer acceptance of wet cake and required drying, purification, activation, or carbonization preparation

assumptions: The economics tool used fictional wet-feedstock assumptions of 36000.0 / 40000.0 / 43000.0 t/yr and moisture assumptions of 40.0 / 35.0 / 30.0% of wet mass across its scenarios.
The economics tool treated dry mass as 26000.0 t/yr dry in the base case, with conservative and optimistic dry-mass values of 21600.0 and 30100.0 t/yr.
The economics tool made no default assumption for availability fraction, product yield, product price, or variable costs.

The pathway is assessed as a portfolio of carbon-fiber, hard-carbon, and activated-carbon applications; the compatibility score is driven by the checked carbon-fiber requirements and does not establish compatibility for every subapplication.
Assessment assumes specialized downstream processing and qualification would be supplied by external partners or new facilities.
uncertainties: The indicative economics could not calculate usable feedstock, product output, revenue, variable cost, gross contribution, or contribution per tonne because required inputs were missing.
The compatibility score of 1 reflects carbon-fiber checks and may not represent activated-carbon compatibility, for which precursor quality has no strict limitations.
The TRL 5 evidence applies to lignin precursor fiber production and does not establish readiness for every carbon-material subapplication.
Unknown ash, volatiles, carbohydrates, metals, particles, and carbon yield could materially change product suitability and processing cost.
No evidence confirms that Pinecrest's wet cake can enter any carbon-material process without drying.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: Activated carbon offers the least restrictive documented precursor route, but the overall pathway still requires drying and downstream carbonization or activation, while carbon-fiber use shows a compatibility score of 1 and battery materials can require a 3-year qualification cycle. Pinecrest therefore needs major new processing assets and partners, with no established buyer route identified.

decision.ranking_source: score_and_rank, called by the Decision Agent

main_drivers: Highest ranked pathway with attractiveness 2.19 and range 1.95–2.75, despite only 0.8 assessed weight.
Market evidence and technical readiness each score 3, supported by industrially relevant development and TRL 5 evidence.
Commercialization feasibility scores 2 because drying, carbonization or activation, qualification, and external partners are needed.
Feedstock compatibility scores 1 for the checked carbon-fiber requirements; this check may not represent activated-carbon compatibility.
Indicative economics was not assessed, so the ranking is provisional; evidence quality is high-to-moderate with two high and two moderate cited records.
what_could_change_it: A measured Pinecrest assay for ash, volatiles, residual carbohydrates, metals, particles, and carbon yield could improve or reduce suitability and processing cost.
A demonstrated wet-cake acceptance route, or a buyer specification requiring drying, could materially change commercialization feasibility.
A sourced product price, yield, variable-cost estimate, and availability fraction could establish indicative economics and move the pathway up or down.
A commercial qualification result or purchase commitment for activated carbon, carbon fiber, or battery materials could improve market evidence and feasibility.
Evidence that the carbon-fiber compatibility gap applies broadly across the pathway could move it down; evidence that activated-carbon requirements are met could move it up.

main_drivers: Listed as insufficient data rather than ranked because only 0.55 of the weight was assessed; feedstock compatibility and indicative economics were not assessed.
Technical readiness scores 5, and market evidence scores 3, reflecting high reported readiness and established industrial adhesive use without documented Pinecrest qualification or named buyers.
Commercialization feasibility scores 2 because activation or depolymerization, drying or wet-cake acceptance, qualification, and external partners are needed.
The reported attractiveness is 3.45 with a wide range of 2.35–4.15, underscoring that it is not comparable to the ranked result as a settled ranking.
Evidence quality is high-to-moderate, with one high and one moderate cited record.
what_could_change_it: Numeric PF requirements matched against Pinecrest molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, ash, and sodium could allow feedstock compatibility to be scored.
A measured availability fraction, product yield, product price, and variable-cost estimate could assess economics and determine whether this pathway ranks above carbon materials.
A resin or panel producer's stated interest in wet cake, or an identified buyer drying arrangement to be evaluated, could improve commercialization feasibility.
A Pinecrest-specific resin formulation, qualification trial, or conditional offtake discussion could raise market evidence and reduce commercialization uncertainty.
Evidence of costly drying, chemical modification, or boiler-fuel displacement could move it down.

what_could_change_it: A measured total hydroxyl value and other formulation-relevant properties could enable compatibility testing, particularly for rigid-foam requirements.

validation_steps.action: Verify Pinecrest moisture and dry-mass availability, then quantify the portion that can be diverted from boiler fuel and dispatched reliably from limited covered storage.
validation_steps.reason: This establishes the usable feedstock basis and addresses moisture, storage, diversion, and availability uncertainties affecting all pathways.

validation_steps.action: Commission a feedstock assay covering molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl or total hydroxyl value, sodium, ash, volatiles, residual carbohydrates, metals, particles, and carbon yield.
validation_steps.reason: These are the principal missing qualification inputs and would enable pathway-specific compatibility testing rather than treating missing evidence as poor performance.

validation_steps.action: Obtain route-specific process and economic quotations from qualified partners, including drying, activation or depolymerization, modification, carbonization, yield, variable costs, and product specifications.
validation_steps.reason: The scoring engine could not assess indicative economics for any pathway because availability fraction, product yield, product price, and variable costs were missing.

validation_steps.action: Run representative Pinecrest samples through customer qualification trials with a panel-resin producer, polyurethane formulator, and carbon-material processor.
validation_steps.reason: Trials would test actual performance, wet-cake or drying acceptance, preparation requirements, and Pinecrest-specific qualification beyond broad pathway TRL evidence.

validation_steps.action: Seek non-binding buyer feedback on delivered price, volume, regional demand, acceptance specifications, and qualification timeline.
validation_steps.reason: The current assessment lacks named buyers, contracts, current prices, and demand; structured market feedback could substantially change market evidence and economics without implying demand is established.

ranking_changers: Completing indicative economics for all pathways—especially availability fraction, product yield, product price, and variable costs—could materially change the current provisional outcome.

A Pinecrest-specific compatibility assay could either validate phenolic resins or polyurethane, or confirm the carbon-fiber gap and narrow carbon materials to a more suitable subapplication such as activated carbon.
A buyer willing to evaluate wet cake, or an economical drying and processing partner, would directly improve the feasibility of routes currently constrained by the lack of mill assets.
A purchase commitment or successful customer qualification would provide stronger market evidence than the current pilot, industrial-use, and research evidence.
The existing boiler-fuel value and the cost of diverting and drying the wet cake could materially change the commercial case for every external-sales pathway.
caveats: The Pinecrest feedstock and dashboard project are explicitly fictional.
Carbon materials is the only pathway ranked by the deterministic engine. Phenolic resins and polyurethanes are listed as insufficient data, not as lower-scoring ranked alternatives.
Attractiveness, data completeness, and evidence quality are separate: missing criteria were not scored as poor performance.
Indicative economics was not calculated for any pathway because availability fraction, product yield, product price, and variable costs were missing.
The carbon-materials compatibility score of 1 reflects checked carbon-fiber requirements and may not represent activated-carbon compatibility.
No numeric feedstock compatibility test was available for phenolic resins or polyurethanes.
The assessment does not calculate usable feedstock, product output, revenue, variable cost, gross contribution, or contribution per tonne.
The ranking depends on broad pathway evidence and does not establish commercial qualification of Pinecrest lignin.
report.summary: Carbon materials is the deterministic engine's rank-1 pathway at 2.19, but the result is provisional because economics is unassessed and carbon-fiber compatibility is weak. Phenolic resins and polyurethanes remain insufficient-data pathways rather than ranked losers; both could move substantially after feedstock assays, economics, and buyer qualification. The next priority is to verify moisture and diversion volume, characterize the cake, complete route economics, and run customer trials.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
Replacing 25% of the polyol with lignin cut compressive strength by 40% compared with lignin-free foam; raising lignin from 25% to 60% caused no further drop.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Softwood lignin gives high carbon yields (55% or more) but is not readily melt-spinnable without a plasticizing agent; hardwood lignin is the reverse, with slightly lower yield (50-55%).
Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
